### Tutorial 7.2: Building a CVP Model for a Charles River Furniture Line

**Context and objective.** You will build a cost-volume-profit model for the Beacon extension dining table, one of the furniture lines that Charles River manufactures in-house. Using the item's list price and standard cost from the Item table, along with estimated fixed costs, you will calculate the break-even point, build a profit schedule across a range of volumes, and create a chart that visualizes the break-even point.

**Prerequisites.** Open the Charles River dataset in Excel. Navigate to the Item table (in the Master Data group) and locate the Beacon extension dining table, a manufactured Furniture item (its SupplyMode is "Manufactured" and its ItemGroup is "Furniture"). You will need its ListPrice and StandardCost values. The ListPrice represents the selling price, and the StandardCost represents the variable cost per unit for this exercise. If you are working from the SQLite version of the dataset, you can export the relevant rows to Excel using the techniques from Chapter 4, or you can use the values shown in the steps below.

**Step 1.** Create a new worksheet and name it "CVP_DiningTable." In cell A1, type "Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis: Beacon Dining Table" as a title. Leave row 2 blank. In cell A3, type "Assumptions" and format it as a section header (bold, larger font).

**Step 2.** Enter the assumption labels and values. In cell A4, type "Selling Price per Unit" and in cell B4, enter the ListPrice for the item, which is approximately $1,850. In cell A5, type "Variable Cost per Unit" and in cell B5, enter the StandardCost, which is approximately $1,040. In cell A6, type "Fixed Costs (Estimated)" and in cell B6, enter 245000. This is an estimated value representing the fixed manufacturing overhead, selling expenses, and administrative costs allocated to the furniture line for the quarter. In cell A7, type "Contribution Margin per Unit" and in cell B7, enter the formula =B4-B5. In cell A8, type "Contribution Margin Ratio" and in cell B8, enter the formula =B7/B4. Format B8 as a percentage.

**Step 3.** Calculate the break-even point. In cell A10, type "Break-Even Analysis" and format it as a section header. In cell A11, type "Break-Even Volume (Units)" and in cell B11, enter the formula =ROUNDUP(B6/B7, 0). This divides total fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit and rounds up because you cannot sell a fraction of a dining table. In cell A12, type "Break-Even Revenue" and in cell B12, enter the formula =B11*B4.

**Step 4.** Build a volume-profit schedule. In cell A14, type "Volume-Profit Schedule" as a section header. In cell A15, type "Quantity" and in cells B15 through H15, type "Revenue," "Variable Cost," "Fixed Cost," "Total Cost," "Profit," "Margin %," and "Cumulative Profit."

**Step 5.** In cells A16 through A31, enter quantities from 50 to 800 in increments of 50. This range should include values below, at, and above the break-even point so the schedule illustrates the transition from loss to profit.

**Step 6.** In cell B16, enter the revenue formula =A16*$B$4. The dollar signs create an absolute reference to the selling price cell so the formula can be copied down without the reference shifting. In cell C16, enter =A16*$B$5 for total variable cost. In cell D16, enter =$B$6 for fixed cost (which does not change with volume). In cell E16, enter =C16+D16 for total cost. In cell F16, enter =B16-E16 for profit. In cell G16, enter =F16/B16 for the profit margin percentage. In cell H16, enter =F16 for cumulative profit (this will be more meaningful in a multi-product context but illustrates the concept here).

**Step 7.** Copy the formulas in row 16 down through row 31. Format the Revenue, Variable Cost, Fixed Cost, Total Cost, and Profit columns as currency. Format the Margin % column as percentage. Examine the Profit column and confirm that it transitions from negative (loss) to positive (profit) as volume increases. The row where profit first becomes positive should correspond closely to the break-even volume calculated in Step 3.

**Step 8.** Create a break-even chart. Select the Quantity column (A15:A31) and the Revenue and Total Cost columns (B15:B31 and E15:E31). Insert a line chart (Insert tab, Line chart). Revenue and Total Cost should appear as two lines. The point where they cross is the break-even point. Add a chart title "Break-Even Analysis: Beacon Dining Table" and label the axes "Units Sold" and "Dollars."

*[Figure 7.9: Break-even chart for the Beacon dining table furniture line. Two lines cross: the Revenue line (ascending from the origin) and the Total Cost line (ascending from the fixed cost level). The break-even point is marked where the two lines intersect, with an annotation showing the break-even volume and revenue.]*

**Step 9.** Add a data label or annotation at the break-even point. You can do this by inserting a text box on the chart and typing the break-even volume and revenue, or by adding a data point at the exact break-even quantity.

**Checkpoint.** Your CVP_DiningTable worksheet should contain three sections: Assumptions (selling price, variable cost, fixed costs, contribution margin), Break-Even Analysis (break-even volume and revenue), and the Volume-Profit Schedule (quantities from 50 to 800 with all six calculated columns). The break-even volume should be approximately 303 units (245,000 divided by the contribution margin of approximately 810 per unit). The break-even chart should clearly show the crossover point. All formulas in the schedule should reference the assumption cells, so that changing any assumption value immediately updates the entire analysis.

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> Cost accountants in manufacturing companies routinely build CVP models during the annual planning cycle to evaluate pricing proposals and production plans. The best models separate assumptions from calculations exactly as described in this tutorial, because the planning process involves multiple rounds of revision as pricing, cost, and volume estimates are refined. A model that hard-codes values requires manual updates at every step, while a model built with cell references to an assumptions section updates instantly.
